summary: CODEC proposes applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to neural network contribution spaces (rather than activation spaces) to decompose coordinated neuronal effects into interpretable modes, with validation on ResNet-50, ViT-B, and biological CNN models of the retina. The dual artificial/biological framing is novel and the causal motivation is principled, but the paper is substantially weakened by the near-complete absence of statistical significance reporting, limited architectural breadth in the main text, and inadequate positioning against the recent wave of SAE-based mechanistic interpretability work. The core contribution is meaningful and incrementally advances the field, but the experimental rigor falls short of ICLR acceptance standards as submitted.
strengths: The core distinction between analyzing contributions (causal, projective-field-aware) versus activations (purely receptive-field) is well-motivated, clearly explained, and drives a genuinely different signal — Fig. 3's finding that contributions decorrelate positive/negative components across depth is an interesting empirical discovery.

The dual-domain application — applying CODEC to state-of-the-art CNN models of the vertebrate retina (Ding et al. 2023) — is a notable differentiator relative to pure ANN interpretability papers; the resulting hypotheses about retinal interneuron modes and dynamic receptive fields (Fig. 8) are experimentally testable and scientifically meaningful.

The ablation/preservation experiment framework (Fig. 6) is a direct causal test of mode utility and is stronger evidence than correlation-only evaluations; comparing contribution modes, activation modes, and random channels for the same task is appropriate experimental design.
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Figs. S3/S4) and training details (epochs, LR, batch size, GPU type) are provided, giving a reasonable foundation for reproducibility.
Extending CODEC to ViT-B across three distinct layer types (token features, MLPs, attention) shows architectural breadth beyond CNNs, even if preliminary.

key_concerns.issue: No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests appear on any quantitative result in the main paper. Key claims — that contribution modes are more class-correlated than activation modes (Fig. 5), that ablation is more effective for contribution modes vs. activation modes (Fig. 6D/E), that contributions are sparser than activations (Fig. 3B) — all require variance estimates across seeds, images, or bootstrap resamples to be believable at ICLR. A single R² point of 0.85 with no variance is uninterpretable.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report mean ± standard deviation or 95% CIs for all main quantitative comparisons. Run SAE training with at least 3 random seeds and aggregate. For the ablation/preservation curves (Fig. 6D), show standard error bands across the 1000 ImageNet classes or across multiple random subsamples.

key_concerns.issue: The paper is substantially under-positioned against the recent mechanistic interpretability literature on SAEs applied to neural networks (e.g., published work on SAE dictionaries for LLM features, monosemanticity research, and related activation decomposition methods). The key technical novelty is applying SAEs to contribution vectors rather than activation vectors, but this incremental step is not clearly contrasted against that body of work, leaving the contribution ambiguous.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a dedicated comparison subsection in Related Work explicitly addressing SAE-based interpretability of activations; articulate precisely which properties of contribution spaces (vs. activation spaces) make SAE decomposition qualitatively different in behavior or downstream utility.

key_concerns.issue: Main-text experiments are essentially limited to ResNet-50 on ImageNet; the ViT-B results are relegated to a brief paragraph with key details deferred to supplementary. For a method claimed to be 'architecturally agnostic,' one additional well-characterized architecture (e.g., EfficientNet, a ResNeXt) with full main-text results is needed.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Promote ViT results to main text with at least the class-correlation and ablation comparisons shown for CNNs, or add a second CNN architecture. If ViT performance is 'inferior,' quantify the gap and diagnose it explicitly rather than attributing it broadly to 'lack of spatial equivariant bias.'

key_concerns.issue: The ablation/preservation case study focuses substantially on the 'black widow' class; while Fig. 6D/E shows results aggregated over blocks, the reader cannot tell whether the contribution-vs-activation advantage is consistent across classes or driven by a few easy cases. The paper claims CODEC 'more reliably identified necessary and sufficient channels' but the evidence supporting 'reliably' across diverse classes is thin in the main paper.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Show the distribution (histogram or box plot) of per-class performance scores (Fig. 6E's metric) for contribution modes vs. activation modes across all 1000 classes; report the fraction of classes where contribution modes outperform activation modes.

key_concerns.issue: The choice of 10 integration steps for Integrated Gradients is well below the commonly recommended 50–300 steps, and the completeness guarantee of IG degrades noticeably at 10 steps for spatially complex images. This could systematically understate contribution quality relative to what more accurate IG would yield.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include a supplementary analysis showing that key results (sparsity, class-correlation, ablation performance) are stable as integration steps vary from 10 to 100+; or justify 10 steps via convergence diagnostics.

key_concerns.issue: The 'causal' language used throughout (title, abstract, body) is stronger than what the method formally supports. IG-based contributions satisfy attribution axioms (completeness, sensitivity) but do not guarantee interventional causality in the Pearl/Rubin sense; ablation experiments add some causal evidence but are not formally equivalent.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Qualify 'causal' with appropriate hedging (e.g., 'attribution-based causal influence' or 'interventionally validated attribution'); the ablation experiments are already the best evidence for causal claims, so lean on those rather than IG alone.

questions_for_authors: The SAE reconstruction R² of 0.85 (contributions) vs. 0.84 (activations) is nearly identical — why is a similar reconstruction quality consistent with the claim that contribution modes are substantially more class-correlated? What specific property of the contribution distribution (rather than reconstruction quality) drives the improved class correlation?

How sensitive are the contribution sparsity results (Fig. 3B) and mode class-correlations (Fig. 5) to the choice of contribution algorithm? SmoothGrad and ActGrad are compared for spatial sparsity (Supplementary Fig. S1A) but the SAE decomposition results in the main paper use only Integrated Gradients — do contribution modes derived from ActGrad yield comparable class-correlations?

For the retina application, the contribution target is changed to surprisal (self-information of the population response) rather than top logit — how does this choice affect CODEC's behavior, and would using a simpler single-cell target (e.g., the firing rate of one ganglion cell) give qualitatively different modes?

The paper notes that mode performance in ViTs is 'inferior' to CNNs — can you provide quantitative numbers (e.g., the Fig. 6E-style performance score for ViT vs. ResNet) to characterize how large the gap is and whether contribution modes still outperform activation modes in ViTs?

Are the three clusters identified by k-means in the retina analysis (Fig. 8C) robust to the number of clusters chosen, beyond the silhouette-value justification for k=3? What do these clusters correspond to biologically (e.g., ON vs. OFF vs. ON-OFF cells)?
calibration_check: Claims are generally reasonably scoped to the evidence presented — the paper appropriately disclaims LLM scaling to supplementary and notes ViT limitations — but the repeated use of 'causal' framing throughout overreaches what attribution-based methods formally establish, and the central 'more reliable' claim about contribution modes requires statistical support currently absent.

significance.justification: The contribution-vs-activation distinction is meaningful and the dual biological/artificial framing is a genuine differentiator, but the practical impact is incremental relative to the growing SAE interpretability ecosystem.

novelty.justification: Applying SAEs to contribution vectors rather than activation vectors is the core technical advance — a meaningful but modest step; the retina application is more novel, but the ANN side builds directly on established IG + SAE infrastructure.

rigor.justification: The experimental design (ablation/preservation with contribution vs. activation baselines) is conceptually sound, but the absence of statistical tests and over-reliance on a single architecture and single illustrative class weaken the evidentiary chain.

statistical_soundness.justification: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear on any main-paper quantitative claim; single-seed SAE results with R² point estimates are insufficient for ICLR-level claims about method superiority.

calibration_honesty.justification: The limitations section is reasonably honest about scope restrictions and the LLM disclaimer is appropriate, but 'causal' language in the title and throughout the paper is not fully backed by the attribution-based methodology.

clarity.justification: The high-level motivation is clear and well-written, but the contribution-mapping equations in the visualization section are dense and the notation is introduced without sufficient scaffolding for readers unfamiliar with Jacobian decompositions.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows standard conference structure well, the abstract accurately previews the contributions, and length is appropriate; the splitting of ViT results to supplementary is a minor structural weakness.

reproducibility.justification: Core hyperparameters and architecture details are described, and training time is reported, but the 10-step IG choice is non-standard, the SAE architecture (MLP size) is only partially specified in the main text, and key implementation details are spread across supplementary sections.

related_work.justification: The saliency and attribution literature is covered adequately, but the recent mechanistic interpretability literature on SAE-based activation decomposition — directly relevant to the core method — is conspicuously absent, leaving the contribution poorly delineated.

figure_quality.justification: From captions, the figures appear well-designed: layerwise evolution plots, SAE loading examples, ablation curves with appropriate baselines, and retina IRF visualizations all map directly onto the paper's claims and are not merely decorative.

breadth_generality.justification: Main-text results are almost entirely on ResNet-50/ImageNet; ViT results are preliminary and confined to supplementary; only vision tasks are addressed; the claim of an 'architecturally agnostic' framework is not adequately demonstrated with the experiments provided.

overall_recommendation.justification: The paper offers a principled and interesting contribution — reframing interpretability around SAE-decomposed contributions rather than activations, with a compelling biological application — but the statistical rigor, architectural breadth, and related-work positioning are below the ICLR acceptance bar as submitted.
